rationale: Start with a broad, moderately fast gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds.

Increase temperature while holding the gradient fixed to probe selectivity of the single critical pair at R = 0.62. The current elution window leaves ample room below the 10-minute time-penalty threshold.
Test a smaller temperature increase to improve the central critical pair while checking whether the neighboring pair, whose resolution declined at 50 C, remains acceptable.

Use a shallower gradient at 50 C to improve the R = 0.89 pair without the neighboring selectivity loss seen at 55 C. The substantial time margin should allow greater separation before the last peak reaches 10 minutes.

A modestly shallower gradient at 55 C may separate the early critical pair while preserving the central pair near R = 1.5. This tests the balance between the opposing temperature and gradient-selectivity effects without approaching the time penalty.
Extend the gradient one step to bring the R = 1.47 pair above 1.5. The other critical pair changed little between 10 and 12 minutes, and the last peak should remain below 10 minutes.

The maximum CRF is secured; now seek a shorter fully resolved method. This slope lies between those of injections 5 and 6, which should lift the R = 1.47 pair above threshold while eluting the last peak sooner than injection 6.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 7, between the nearly resolved and fully resolved settings. This should shorten the elution window while retaining full resolution, with the final organic fraction still sufficient for the last peak.

With maximum CRF secured, test a cooler, steeper-gradient alternative for a shorter fully resolved run. Cooling may separate the central compounds on the opposite side of their temperature-dependent elution-order crossover.

Return to the favorable 55 C selectivity and lower the starting organic fraction to test whether additional early retention permits a faster gradient. Compare the two central critical pairs with the fully resolved injection 8.

Reduce the slope slightly from injection 10 to raise the R = 1.37 pair above threshold while monitoring the marginal R = 1.53 pair. This may achieve full resolution with an earlier last peak than injection 8.

Test a substantially faster gradient at 60 C for an alternative fully resolved elution order. The earlier temperature trend suggests the critical early pair may cross and separate again, while the central pair benefits from higher temperature.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction and gentler slope can improve the two critical pairs in the fast 60 C method. This explores a different selectivity balance while retaining a short elution window.

Test whether the steeper gradient improves the central critical pair at 50 C, reversing the deterioration seen when the gradient was lengthened. Lowering temperature from injection 12 should also move the earlier critical pair away from its high-temperature crossover.

Probe an intermediate cooler temperature with a moderately shallower gradient to seek a second fully resolved selectivity window. This avoids the severe crowding at 25 C while testing separation on the cooler side of the central elution-order changes.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a compensating shallower slope at the successful 55 C temperature. This will show whether shifting the gradient window can preserve both critical separations while shortening retention.

Lengthen injection 16 by one grid step to improve its sole unresolved pair while retaining the central pair's larger resolution margin. This may provide a fully resolved alternative with better minimum resolution and no time penalty.

Shorten the programmed gradient while preserving the slope of fully resolved injection 11. Its last peak should elute before the gradient ends at the outlet, so the lower endpoint should retain CRF 1.000.

Increase the endpoint one grid step from injection 18 to test the faster boundary of the fully resolved region. The early critical pair is most likely to fall below 1.5; injection 18 remains the fallback if it does.

Test a modestly shallower gradient at 40 C to separate the central pair on the cooler side of its elution-order crossover. Injection 1 had only one unresolved pair, making this a focused alternative to the narrow fully resolved region at 55 C.

Reduce the endpoint one step from injection 17 to bring its R = 1.41 pair above threshold while preserving the other critical pair's margin. This targets another maximum-score method with a potentially stronger minimum resolution and a last peak below 10 minutes.

Raise temperature one step from the shortest fully resolved method to test whether retention can be shortened without losing full resolution. This directly checks the temperature boundary at the successful low-starting-organic gradient.

Return to 55 C and increase the endpoint one step from injection 6 to shorten retention while preserving full resolution. The resulting slope lies between two successful settings, making this a low-risk refinement of the maximum-score region.

Shorten the programmed gradient by another step while preserving injection 18's slope through the critical separations. The final peak will encounter the hold, so this tests whether the shorter program still achieves full resolution with its last peak below 10 minutes.

With CRF 1.000 already secured, use the final injection to test a larger resolution margin by slightly reducing the slope from injection 21 while keeping the predicted last peak below 10 minutes. Injection 18 remains the preferred shorter fully resolved method.
